d.title: Four families, sorted by what each one needs and cannot see
d.caption: The families are not ranked by quality — they are ranked by **what you have to supply**. Intrinsic metrics need only the model's own probabilities and are blind to whether the content is true. Reference-based metrics need a written gold answer per case, which is what caps the eval set, and are blind to a correct answer worded differently. Model-based metrics need a judge you have **validated**, and behavioural metrics need a checkable outcome and tell you nothing about why it failed.

cells.text: why it failed, without the trace

d.title: Two forms of one formula, and the commonest implementation bug
d.caption: Perplexity is the **exponential of the cross-entropy** — that is the whole definition. Natural log with `exp`, or log base 2 with a power of 2: the same number either way, and **mixing them is the commonest implementation bug**, producing a figure that is wrong by a factor of ln 2 in the exponent. Worked on four tokens: the mean log₂ p is −1.75, so perplexity is 2^1.75 = 3.3636.

d.title: Three ways perplexity lies
d.caption: All three are the same structural problem: perplexity is a statement about **a model, a tokenizer and a corpus together**, and it gets quoted as a statement about the model alone. A bigger vocabulary splits text into fewer tokens and changes the number without changing quality. Perplexity on Wikipedia and on legal contracts are different numbers about different things. And a low figure on an instruction-tuned model says nothing about helpfulness.

items.label: Not across tokenizers
items.sub: a bigger vocabulary gives fewer tokens - the number moves, the model does not

items.label: Not across datasets
items.sub: Wikipedia and legal contracts are different numbers about different things

items.label: Not a quality measure
items.sub: low perplexity is not helpfulness, safety or correctness

d.title: BLEU is a geometric mean of clipped precisions, times a length penalty
d.caption: Three pieces, each doing one job. **Modified n-gram precision** counts matches with each reference n-gram usable only as often as it appears — the clipping of §03. The **geometric mean** across n = 1 to 4 means a zero at any order drives the whole score to zero, which is why BLEU is harsh on short candidates. And the **brevity penalty** exists because precision alone rewards saying less: a one-word candidate that happens to match scores 1.0 without it.

nodes.label: BP x exp(sum of w_n log p_n)

d.title: BLEU-4 worked through, every intermediate
d.caption: Note how the clipping bites: at n=2 the candidate has 4 bigrams and only **3 survive clipping**, and at n=4 only 1 of 2. The geometric mean of the four precisions is 0.7071, the brevity penalty for a 5-token candidate against a 6-token reference is 0.818731, and the product is **0.578930**. Every figure reproduces the published one to four decimal places.

d.title: Why clipping exists, in one candidate
d.caption: Take `"the the the the the"` against a reference containing `"the"` twice. **Unclipped, all five candidate unigrams appear in the reference, so precision is 1.0** — a perfect score for a string that says nothing. Clipping caps the count at how often the n-gram appears in the reference, giving 2/5. That is the entire reason for the `min(count_candidate, count_reference)` term, and it generalises: clipping is what stops a precision metric rewarding repetition.

nodes.label: Unclipped precision: 1.0
nodes.sub: all five appear in the reference

d.title: Four variants, and what each unit is sensitive to
d.caption: One formula, four units. **ROUGE-1 measures content overlap and nothing about order** — which is why a shuffled sentence scores identically. ROUGE-2 brings in local ordering through bigrams. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence, so it captures sentence structure **without requiring contiguity**: words can be interrupted and still count, which is closer to what a human means by "same shape".

d.title: The same pair, scored by ROUGE instead of BLEU
d.caption: The identical candidate-reference pair that gave BLEU-4 of 0.578930 gives **ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.9091**. Both numbers are correct and they are measuring different things: BLEU's geometric mean punishes the weak 4-gram precision, and ROUGE-1 rewards the perfect unigram precision. Which is the practical reason to report both or neither — quoting whichever is higher is a choice, not a measurement. Note ROUGE-L matches ROUGE-1 exactly here, because the LCS happens to be all five candidate tokens in order.

d.title: Three fixes for n-gram overlap, at three prices
d.caption: Each one targets a specific failure of exact matching. **METEOR matches on stems and synonyms**, so a correct paraphrase stops scoring zero — at the cost of needing language resources, which is why it is rarely used outside English. **chrF works on character n-grams and needs no tokenizer at all**, which makes it robust to morphology and typos and almost free. BERTScore replaces matching with cosine similarity in embedding space, and needs a model pass per evaluation.

d.title: BERTScore's greedy matching is not one-to-one, and that matters
d.caption: Each candidate token independently takes its **best** reference match, so two candidate tokens may claim the same reference token. An optimal one-to-one assignment — the Hungarian algorithm — would forbid that, and BERTScore does not use one. The practical consequence: **a repetitive candidate is not penalised the way BLEU's clipping penalises it.** Repeating a well-matching token raises precision because each copy finds the same good match again.

d.title: Three metrics for constrained output
d.caption: These are the cheapest metrics in the module and the ones with no judge, no reference model and no ambiguity — **provided the output is genuinely constrained**. Exact match is right for extraction, classification and structured fields, and the words *after normalisation* in its definition are doing almost all of the work, which §02 is about. Token F1 is the fallback for short answers where the wording varies slightly.
cells: harmonic mean of token P and R

d.title: Without normalisation the metric is measuring formatting
d.caption: Lowercase, strip punctuation, strip articles, collapse whitespace — four operations, and without them **`"The Answer."` and `"answer"` are different strings**. A model that is right every time then scores zero, and what you have built is a formatting checker wearing a correctness metric's name. Which is why every serious QA benchmark publishes its normaliser alongside its data: the normaliser *is* part of the metric.

d.title: Three predictions, exact match 0.0 every time
d.caption: All three say the right thing and **all three score exact match 0.0**. Token F1 separates them usefully: adding a harmless word costs little (0.8889), spelling the number differently costs more (0.7500), and **reordering costs nothing at all — 1.0000**, because F1 treats both strings as bags of tokens. That last row is the limitation to keep in mind: token F1 cannot see word order, so `"per year 18 days"` is a perfect answer by this metric.

d.title: pass@k read in words
d.caption: **1 minus the probability that all k chosen samples come from the failing pile.** The numerator counts ways to choose k failures from the n − c failures; the denominator counts ways to choose k from all n. On n=10 with c=7 the four figures reproduce the published ones exactly — and note pass@5 already reads 1.0000, which §02 explains is a boundary effect rather than a result.

d.title: Why n must exceed k, and by how much
d.caption: At **n=10 and k=10 the estimator must return 1.0000 whenever c ≥ 1** — drawing all ten samples necessarily includes the one that passed, so the number carries no information. Raise n to 100 at the same 5% pass rate and pass@10 reads **0.4162**, which is a real estimate. The last row confirms it is the *ratio* that matters rather than the absolute n: doubling both n and c leaves the estimates essentially unchanged.

d.title: Five queries with graded relevance, which is what the order-aware metrics need
d.caption: Binary relevance supports precision, recall and MRR. **Graded relevance — a 0 to 3 scale — is what NDCG needs**, because a rank-weighted gain has to know how much each document is worth. The dataset here deliberately varies the number of relevant documents per query, from 1 to 4, which is what makes §05's scoreboard instructive: the per-query metrics behave very differently depending on how many relevant documents there were to find.

nodes.label: So the metrics diverge per query

d.title: Precision is not monotonic; recall only ever climbs
d.caption: Walking down the ranking, **precision jumps at every hit and decays at every miss** — 0.5000, 0.3333, 0.5000, 0.4000, 0.3333, 0.4286 — so precision@5 and precision@10 can disagree about which retriever is better. **Recall only ever climbs**, and flattens permanently once the last relevant chunk is found: it is 1.0000 from k=7 onwards and still 1.0000 at k=50. That makes recall a hard bound rather than a curve, and makes the choice of k a precision decision.

d.title: Four order-aware metrics, and what each one is really asking
d.caption: These exist because precision and recall at a cutoff are blind to **where** inside the cutoff a document landed. Reciprocal rank asks only about the **first** hit, which makes it the right metric when one good answer is enough and the wrong one when coverage matters. Average precision averages precision at every hit, so it rewards getting *all* of them early. R-precision uses the number of relevant documents as the cutoff, which removes the arbitrary k.

d.title: Two standard gain functions, and NDCG figures that are not comparable
d.caption: This module uses **linear** gain and module 5 uses **exponential** gain. Neither is wrong — both are standard — and **their NDCG figures are not comparable with each other**. Exponential gain weights a grade-3 document seven times a grade-1 one; linear weights it three times. At binary relevance the two coincide, since 2¹−1 = 1 and 2⁰−1 = 0; on a 0–3 scale they differ by 1.5 points here, and the gap widens with the scale. So "NDCG@6 = 0.96" is not a comparable figure across two teams unless both state the gain function.

nodes.label: On 0-3 they differ by 1.5 points
nodes.sub: and the gap widens with the scale

d.title: The scoreboard, and the two queries that diagnose themselves
d.caption: Read across the rows rather than down the columns. **Q2 has AP 1.0000 and RR 1.0000** — both relevant documents at the top, a perfect retrieval. **Q3 has RR 0.1111**, meaning its single relevant document sat at rank 9, so P@5 is 0.0000 and R@5 is 0.0000 while R@10 is 1.0000: a complete failure at k=5 and a complete success at k=10, from one document's position. The means at the bottom average all of that away.
